objectives: Apply Bernoulli + the mechanical energy balance.
Use Reynolds number to predict flow regime.
Distinguish heat, mass, momentum transport analogies.

slides.title: Mechanical energy balance + pipe-flow design
slides.body:
For incompressible isothermal pipe flow between points 1 + 2:

  (P₁/ρ + v₁²/2 + g z₁) + W_pump = (P₂/ρ + v₂²/2 + g z₂) + h_f

The **friction loss** h_f along a pipe of length L + diameter D is:

  h_f = (4 f) (L/D) (v²/2)

where **f** is the Fanning friction factor (or use Darcy = 4 × Fanning if you see f_D in formulas).

For laminar flow (Re < 2100): f = 16/Re (analytical, Hagen-Poiseuille).
For turbulent flow (Re > 4000): f from Moody chart or Colebrook equation:
  1/√f = −4 log₁₀(ε/D/3.7 + 1.26/(Re √f))

Key design quantities:
• **Reynolds number** Re = ρ v D / μ — predicts laminar vs turbulent.
• **Volumetric flow rate** Q = v · A = v · πD²/4.
• **Pressure drop** ΔP = h_f · ρ (for horizontal pipe).
• **Pump head** H_pump = W_pump / g — for sizing the pump.

**Pump power**: Ẇ_pump = ṁ · g · H / η = (Q · ρ · g · H) / η, where η is pump efficiency (~60-80% for centrifugals).

**Practical sizing**: economic optimum diameter balances capital cost (~D^1.5) against pumping cost (~D^−5). Typical 'rules of thumb': v ~ 1-3 m/s for liquids, 10-30 m/s for gases. Higher v gives smaller pipe but more pumping.

slides.title: Reynolds number + the dimensionless-number culture
slides.body:
Chemical engineering lives by **dimensionless numbers**. Each is a ratio of physical effects + predicts when one dominates.

• **Re = ρvD/μ** — inertial / viscous. Determines flow regime: laminar (Re<2100), transitional (2100<Re<4000), turbulent (Re>4000). Most industrial flow is turbulent (Re > 10⁴ - 10⁶).
• **Pr = c_p μ / k** — momentum / thermal diffusivity. Gases ~0.7-1; water ~7; oils 50-50000.
• **Sc = μ / (ρD_AB)** — momentum / mass diffusivity. Gases ~0.5-2; liquids ~100-10000.
• **Nu = h L / k** — convective / conductive heat transfer.
• **Sh = k_c L / D_AB** — convective / diffusive mass transfer.
• **Pe = Re · Pr** (heat) or Re · Sc (mass) — convective / diffusive overall.
• **Gr = g β ΔT L³ / ν²** — buoyancy / viscous. Sets natural convection.
• **Ra = Gr · Pr** — full natural convection criterion.
• **We = ρ v² L / σ** — inertial / surface tension. Droplet breakup.
• **Bi = h L / k_s** — external / internal heat transfer. Lumped capacitance valid for Bi << 1.

**Correlations** typically have form: dimensionless transfer coefficient = f(Re, Pr/Sc, geometry).

For turbulent pipe flow:
• **Dittus-Boelter**: Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^0.4 (heating) or Pr^0.3 (cooling).
• **Chilton-Colburn analogy**: Sh = 0.023 Re^0.8 Sc^(1/3).

These collapse hundreds of experimental conditions into one or two equations. The dimensionless-number culture is what makes ChemE quantitative.

slides.title: Heat, mass, momentum transport — the same equations
slides.body:
**Transport phenomena** (Bird, Stewart, Lightfoot 1960) unified the field by recognizing that heat, mass, + momentum transport all obey the same form of equations:

• **Momentum (Newton's law of viscosity)**: τ_yx = −μ ∂v_x/∂y. Shear stress = −μ × velocity gradient.
• **Heat (Fourier's law)**: q_y = −k ∂T/∂y. Heat flux = −k × temperature gradient.
• **Mass (Fick's law)**: J_Ay = −D_AB ∂c_A/∂y. Mass flux = −D_AB × concentration gradient.

Each has a diffusivity (μ/ρ = ν, k/ρc_p = α, D_AB) with units L²/T.

**Boundary-layer theory**: near a solid surface there's a thin region where transport gradients are concentrated. Thickness scales with the appropriate Pr or Sc. For Pr=1 (gases): thermal + velocity BLs coincide. For Pr>1 (liquids): thermal BL is thinner. For Pr<1 (liquid metals): thermal BL is thicker.

**Chilton-Colburn analogy**:
  j_H = (Nu / Re Pr^(1/3)) = (Sh / Re Sc^(1/3)) = j_M = f/2

If you know the friction factor for a geometry, you can predict heat + mass transfer (within ~10%) without independent measurements. Hugely powerful for design.

**Two-resistance model** for interphase transfer (e.g., gas absorber): overall resistance = sum of liquid-side + gas-side resistances. Rate-limiting side dominates; design accordingly.

Modern ChemE process design uses these correlations through equipment-specific design equations: Kern method for shell-and-tube heat exchangers, Sherwood-Holloway for packed columns, etc.

question.question: Design pump head + power for an industrial water transfer
question.goal: Transfer water (ρ=1000 kg/m³, μ=10⁻³ Pa·s) at 50 m³/h from a ground tank to an elevated tank 15 m higher through 200 m of 4-inch (D=0.1 m) commercial steel pipe (roughness ε=4.5×10⁻⁵ m). Both surfaces atmospheric. Pump efficiency 70%.

steps.prompt: Compute velocity in the pipe + Reynolds number.
From the Moody chart / Colebrook, the Fanning friction factor f ≈ 0.005 at Re = 1.77×10⁵, ε/D = 4.5×10⁻⁴. Compute friction head loss h_f in J/kg.
steps.reveal: h_f = 4 × 0.005 × 2000 × 1.566 = 62.6 J/kg. In head units (h_f / g): 6.4 m. Friction loss alone equals ~40% of the static lift.

steps.prompt: Compute the required pump head H_pump (in m of water) from the mechanical energy balance.
steps.motivation: H_pump = Δz + h_f/g (since ΔP = 0 + v in/out negligible).
steps.reveal: H_pump = 15 m + 6.4 m = 21.4 m of water. Pump must provide 21.4 m of head at 50 m³/h.

steps.motivation: Ẇ = Q · ρ · g · H / η.
steps.reveal: Ẇ = 0.0139 × 1000 × 9.81 × 21.4 / 0.70 ≈ 4170 W ≈ 4.2 kW. Pick a 5-kW (or 7.5-kW with margin) centrifugal pump. Capital + operating cost both scale with this number, so it directly drives the project economics.

steps.prompt: What changes if we double the flow rate (100 m³/h)?
steps.motivation: Trace effects through Re, f, h_f, H.
hints: v doubles → Re doubles → f only slightly changes → h_f ∝ v² grows 4×.
steps.reveal: v → 3.54 m/s; Re → 3.54×10⁵ (still turbulent rough); f very slightly drops to ~0.0048 (small effect at this Re). h_f → 4 × 0.0048 × 2000 × 6.27 ≈ 240 J/kg ≈ 24.5 m head. H_pump = 15 + 24.5 = 39.5 m. Power = 0.0278 × 1000 × 9.81 × 39.5 / 0.7 ≈ 15.4 kW — nearly 4× as much as before. The takeaway: pumping power scales roughly with Q³ at fixed pipe geometry. Doubling flow > 3× the power. Pipe sizing has nonlinear effects on operating cost.

question.question: Why does the Reynolds number cleanly separate flow regimes despite the wide variety of fluids + geometries it encompasses?
options: Re = ρvD/μ is the ratio of inertial to viscous forces. When inertia dominates (high Re), small disturbances amplify → turbulence. When viscous forces dominate (low Re), disturbances damp → laminar. The physics of transition (Tollmien-Schlichting waves, secondary instabilities) is set by this ratio, so Re predicts regime universally. The critical value (~2100 for pipe flow) reflects geometry; the principle is dimensionless physics.
It is calibrated empirically + has no physical meaning.
question.explanation:
Reynolds (1883) experimentally observed flow regimes in pipe-tracer experiments + recognized that flow behavior collapsed to a single dimensionless ratio.

Physically: Re = (ρv²) / (μv/D) = inertia / viscous force per unit volume. Or equivalently: Re = (vL) / (μ/ρ) = convection time / diffusion time = how quickly momentum diffuses across the pipe vs how quickly fluid flows along.

**Low Re (laminar)**: viscous diffusion damps disturbances faster than convection amplifies them. Streamlines stable + parallel.
**High Re (turbulent)**: convective amplification wins; small disturbances grow + cascade into a turbulent fluctuation spectrum.

The **critical Reynolds** (~2100 for pipes, ~5×10⁵ for boundary layers) depends on geometry + disturbance level — the transition has a kind of universality similar to a phase transition.

This is why Re works *across* fluids — water, air, glycerol, blood, lava — all have the same regime boundary at the same Re. Same physical mechanism, same dimensionless threshold. **Buckingham Pi theorem** formalizes why dimensionless numbers organize physics so neatly: any dimensionally homogeneous equation can be rewritten in terms of N-K dimensionless groups, where K is the number of fundamental dimensions. The recovered correlations are minimum-redundancy descriptions.

This is why ChemE design is dimensionless-number-driven: it generalizes across scale + fluid.

hints: What's the physical interpretation of Re?
Why is the critical Re consistent across fluids?
slides.workedSolution: Re = ρvD/μ = ratio of inertial to viscous forces. Low Re: viscous damping > convective amplification → stable laminar. High Re: convective amplification > viscous damping → turbulent. Critical Re (~2100 pipes) depends on geometry; the underlying physics is universal (analogous to phase-transition behavior). Buckingham Pi theorem formalizes why dimensionless numbers organize physics. Re predicts regime across all Newtonian fluids + scales — water, air, lava, blood — at the same threshold. Same dimensionless physics, same regime boundary.

question.question: An engineer estimates heat-transfer coefficient h for cooling water flowing in a tube using the Dittus-Boelter correlation: Nu = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^0.4. If Re doubles, how does h change?
options: h scales as Re^0.8 (since Nu = h D / k, and D, k constant). Doubling Re increases h by factor 2^0.8 ≈ 1.74 — a ~74% increase, not 100%. Higher flow rate + smaller pipe both increase h, but with diminishing returns.
question.explanation:
**Dittus-Boelter**: Nu = h D / k = 0.023 Re^0.8 Pr^0.4.

Solving for h: h = 0.023 (k/D) Re^0.8 Pr^0.4. With D, k, fluid properties constant: h ∝ Re^0.8.

Double Re: h ratio = 2^0.8 ≈ 1.74. ~74% increase.

**Practical implications**:
• To enhance heat transfer, increasing velocity is effective but with diminishing returns + costs (pumping power scales as v³).
• Decreasing tube diameter increases h (since Re ∝ v ∝ Q/D² + h ∝ Re^0.8 / D ∝ Q^0.8 / D^1.6) — but at the cost of higher pressure drop (ΔP ∝ Q^1.8 / D^4.8).
• Optimal design balances heat-transfer area + pressure drop + capital cost.

**Why the 0.8 exponent**: in turbulent flow, the heat-transfer boundary layer thickness scales as δ_T ~ D / Re^0.8 (approximate). h ~ k/δ_T ~ k Re^0.8 / D. Empirically tuned to fit data; theoretically derivable from boundary-layer arguments + Reynolds analogy.

**Range of validity**: Re > 10,000, Pr 0.7-160, L/D > 60. Outside this, use other correlations (Sieder-Tate for high Pr, Gnielinski for transitional Re).

Design principle: use the correlation, but know its validity range + uncertainty (~10-20%); compute with sensitivities, not point values.

hints: What does h scale with in Dittus-Boelter?
slides.workedSolution: h = (k/D) × 0.023 × Re^0.8 × Pr^0.4. With D, k, Pr fixed: h ∝ Re^0.8. Doubling Re → h × 2^0.8 ≈ 1.74 → +74%. Practical: higher flow gives diminishing-return heat transfer + cubic pumping cost. Smaller diameter increases h but with major pressure-drop penalty. Design balances area, pressure drop, cost.

question.question: Water (ρ=1000 kg/m³, μ=10⁻³ Pa·s) flows at v=2 m/s in a 5-cm pipe. What's the Reynolds number?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why ChemE relies so heavily on dimensionless correlations (Nu, Re, Pr, Sh, etc.) instead of solving the underlying partial differential equations directly. What's gained, what's lost?
question.rubric: Mentions: full Navier-Stokes + energy + species PDEs are nonlinear + coupled + extremely hard to solve analytically; turbulent flow has no closed-form solution. Dimensionless correlations distill empirical + analytical data into compact + transferable design equations. Gained: rapid design across scales + fluids + geometries (Buckingham Pi); compact predictive relations with ~10-20% accuracy; intuition about which physical effects dominate. Lost: detail of local flow + temperature fields; ability to handle complex geometries; nonlinear coupling beyond what correlations capture. Modern approach: use correlations for first-pass design + economic optimization; CFD / DNS / experiments for detailed verification of critical equipment. The hierarchy reflects engineering pragmatism — fastest accurate-enough tool for each stage.
